title: Beyond Buffer Limits: Energy-Based Data Reassembly for Continual Learning
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Cropping data into patches and assembling them by minimizing a unary-plus-pairwise energy yields compact composite replay samples.
layout: Multi-row flow, top-left to bottom; slot grids, energy-equation callouts, pairwise zoom bubble
description: A flow diagram that starts at top-left with current-task training images, which are cropped into patches. The patches go into an oval list labeled γ_{i,1} to γ_{i,k} and then into a grid of slots z_1, z_2 ... z_S. A rounded callout at top right gives the energy E(z), a unary sum plus a pairwise sum, with a question box asking 'Which patch should be placed here?' and 'arg min E(z)'. A downward arrow leads to a filled composite grid of cat patches with green smiley icons for low pairwise penalty and red prohibition icons for high penalty. An orange zoom bubble on the left shows a red arrow (incompatible patches) and a green arrow (compatible patches). An 'Energy Decomposition' box lists Unary and Pairwise terms. The last arrow leads to a Replay Buffer box holding composite images and a soft-label bar chart.
caption: Illustration of our proposed Energy-Based Data Reassembly method. Unary energy selects label-consistent patches per slot, while interaction energy enforces global coherence across slots, producing compact and informative composite replay images. In contrast to standard memory replay that stores raw images and replays them directly, our method stores energy-reassembled composite images that encode substantially more information than raw images under the same memory budget.
abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to acquire new knowledge from a non-stationary data stream while retaining performance on previously learned tasks. Memory-based replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing and revisiting past samples, but their effectiveness is fundamentally constrained by limited memory capacity, as each stored example represents only a single data instance. In this work, we propose data reassembly for CL, a new paradigm that significantly increases memory efficiency by reassembling composite replay samples from existing training data. Instead of storing raw training examples, we partition the current task training data into elementary patches and dynamically reassemble them into coherent replay instances through an energy-based optimization framework. The proposed objective jointly enforces semantic compatibility with target labels and global consistency among assembled patches. To make this optimization tractable, we derive an efficient variational inference algorithm that constructs a compact yet diverse set of reassembled samples for replay. Extensive theoretical analysis and experiments across multiple CL benchmarks demonstrate that data reassembly consistently outperforms existing memory-based approaches, achieving stronger retention of past knowledge while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.
